## Description of proposed feature
<!-- Add a clear and concise description of the new feature, including a motivation: why do you think this will be useful? -->

### My motivation

Hello, I want to be able to select the last object in a group as the target for alignment when using `Mobject.arrange()`, instead of the default first object.

Like this:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/abd9c835-6a4e-4182-be2c-b71372e7c2a9

### Why

`Mobject.arrange()` always uses the first object as the alignment target:

https://github.com/ManimCommunity/manim/blob/2ab99b53d3e8f43b1cd7245208d78c5dd6f9
Updated the PR to use a `reference` parameter instead of `last`, and fixed the arrange iteration issue. The CI checks are now passing.

I think @behackl's suggestion of "just remember the position of the `reference` mobject, arrange with respect to the first and then shift the arranged group such that the `reference` object is in its original position" (adjusted here for arbitrary reference objects from the group) makes a lot of sense.

But it seems to me that having both the `reference` parameter and the `center` parameter causes issues. If we keep the default of `center=True`, then calling something like `group.arrange(RIGHT, reference=group[-1])` will lead to one of two results, depending on implementation:

1. As is curren

On further reflection: Although this would be a highly breaking change to implement, you _could_ make the argument that it is very unusual for a mobject method to center the mobject after performing the actual change; we wouldn't accept this behavior for methods like `scale` or `rotate`, and AFAIK even `arrange_in_grid` only moves the arranged group back to its original center point, not to ORIGIN. It doesn't seem preposterous that the default behavior of `arrange` would be to keep the first element fixed in space.

This is the same bug as #3005, seen from the other end.

`Scene.compile_animation_data` resets `self.last_t = 0` before every animation and the frame times start at 0 as well, so `update_to_time` works out `dt = 0` for the first frame of each `play()` and `wait()`. Your `upd_circle` shifts by `2 * dt * RIGHT`, so on that one frame the circle does not move, and that is the duplicate you are seeing. The loop is ten animations, so ten stutters, and at 5 fps each one is a fifth of a second wide.

## Description of proposed feature
Support for colors, gradients, and animations utilizing the Oklab and Oklch color models.
These color models account for the fact that color vision is both a physical, and a psychological phenomena.
RGB and HSL/HSV are very easy to implement into computers, but they don't account for some weird biases our vision has.

These perceptual models also represent device-independent color which is very useful for web video. Not every possible input is valid, and the range of possible inputs depends on your target color space (sRGB, P3, Adobe RGB, Rec. 2020, Rec. 2100
The models themselves need not be implemented by the maintainers. Tapping into one of the many pre-existing color libraries in Python should do.

## Description of bug / unexpected behavior
When an Angle is initialized on two lines (even with `always_redraw`) and one of the lines changes the value of the angle doesn't reflect that change.
Might be a duplicate of #3698, if so, can someone please explain?

## Expected behavior
Running `angle.get_value()` should reflect the change in rotation of the lines.

## How to reproduce the issue
<details><summary>Code for reproducing the problem</summary>

Minimal example that just prints the angles to the console while rendering
```py
from manim import *

class Main(Scene):
    def construct(self)

The problem has probably to do with the way how `always_redraw` replaces/updates the object instances.

Here is a quick-and-dirty solution for you (I replaced the `Tex()` with `Text()` so that LaTeX is not evoked for every single frame of the animation with a new value for the angle, and I changed to an f-string with adjustable resolution):
```py
class Main(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        rotation = ValueTracker(0)
        l1 = Line(LEFT, RIGHT)
        l2 = always_redraw(lambda: Line(DOWN, UP).rotate(rotation.get_value()))
        a = always_redraw(lambda: Angle(l1, l2))
        def

Confirmed: `always_redraw` refreshes via `become()`, which copies points/submobjects but not the cached `angle_value` that `get_value()` returns, so it stays at the initial angle. Opened #4853 to copy `angle_value` in an `Angle.become()` override.

## Description of bug / unexpected behavior
Mobjects being drawn to the screen by `TransformFromCopy` with the source mobject being `Text` or `Tex` seem to have no points when `mobject.get_start()` is run and it throws an Exception. I tested it with the source beign some others and it worked fine.

## Expected behavior
Well, it's not supposed to throw an exception...

## How to reproduce the issue
<details><summary>Code for reproducing the problem</summary>

```py
from manim import *

class Main(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        mobject = Circle()
        text = Text("Hello, World!")

There is a dirty fix I found for now but transforming from Text really does not look good imo:
```py
from manim import *

class Main(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        mobject = Circle()
        text = Text("Hello, World!")
        self.add(text)
        temp_mobject = mobject.copy()
        self.play(TransformFromCopy(text, temp_mobject))
        self.add(mobject)
        self.remove(temp_mobject)
        print(f"points: {mobject.get_all_points()}")  # this works fine
        print(f"start: {mobject.get_start()}")  # this now also works
```
It really looks like the transformation messes

Is the text supposed to persist on screen? If not, removing `self.add(text)` will fix that problem.

Regarding the main issue: It will work if you use the OpenGL renderer instead of the default Cairo one, by adding `--renderer opengl` to the CLI command. There's probably some odd renderer-specific behavior going on, either within the Text class itself, or within one of the base classes that the `ConvertToOpenGL` metaclass swaps normal Cairo classes out for.

Root cause: transforming onto a `Text`/`Tex`-shaped mobject leaves the points on submobjects, so the top level has none. `get_start`/`get_end` only checked `self.points` and errored. Opened #4852 to fall back to `family_members_with_points()` (OpenGL already worked because its getters walk the family).

I ran a MoveAlongPath on a parametric function that also raised a RuntimeWarning:
invalid value encountered in scalar power       x = -((2 + t**-3)/(t**3 - 1))**(1/3).
I then also got an exception that said "Not sure how you reached here, please file a bug report at [github link]".

I'm pretty new to manim. I think I just expected it to work lol.

<details><summary>Code for reproducing the problem</summary>

```py
from manim import *

def f(u, v):
    if v == 0:
        return int(bool(u)) # cheati

Hi! At some points in your t_range of [-2, -0.5] (example: t = -1.1), you'll have a negative number raised to the power of 1/3. Python will raise an error when trying to raise a negative number to a decimal number, even if that number is something like 1/3 (trying to calculate the cube root): Python does not store 1/3 as the exact fraction 1/3, but rather a floating point approximation of it, because 1/3 in floating point cannot be expressed as a finite string of 0s and 1s.

In this specific case, apart from a `sqrt` (square root) function, NumPy and the `math` module have `cbrt` (cube root) w
PR #4847 replaces the "Not sure how you reached here" exception with a clear ValueError when the function produces NaN/inf points (and falls back to the last point on float-rounding fallthrough).

## Enhancement proposal
Currently, Manim stores the point data for `VMobjects` as a flat list of points. This is not representative at all of how `VMobjects` are actually structured, i.e. as composite bezier curves. In fact, every four points (three for OpenGL) form the points defining a cubic/bezier curve, yet they are currently not explicitly grouped together. Furthermore, the data of which points form what paths is not stored, and Manim instead spends a significant amount of time every frame checking whether for each pair of consecutive bezier curves, their end and start points are close e

A possible approach is to have a `Bezier` dataclass, then having the `points` array be an array of these dataclasses. This easily extends to allow different path components. If they are made immutable, it will help with caching. However, this might cause overhead when operating on points (I think it would be perfect, if not for that problem).

One possible approach is to have components be subclasses of numpy arrays. Pointwise functions can still be applied directly with numpy through `apply_along_axis`. This could retain speed while semantically splitting up data. Needs more investigation.

I have recently been thinking about this. Calculations of things like subpaths, bounding boxes* and unit normals could be memoized and grouped inside a separate object. For `Mobject`s, it could be something like `MobjectPoints`. For `VMobject`s, it could be a subclass of `MobjectPoints` called `VMobjectPoints`. They would have an underlying `_array` of points, a lot of initially `None` memos for useful things such as subpaths and bounding boxes*, properties / getters which calculate those attributes if they're `None` or return them if they're set to something else, etc. Something like this:

`
